Sacraments (Ordinances)
SAK-ruh-ments
noun / doctrine
From the Latin sacramentum, a sacred oath or pledge; the church’s name for the two ordinances Christ appointed as visible signs and seals of His covenant.

📖 Biblical Definition

The sacraments, more exactly called ordinances, are the two holy signs Christ Himself appointed for His church: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. They are not bare ceremonies but signs and seals of the covenant of grace, by which the benefits of Christ are visibly set forth, and the faith of believers strengthened. Baptism was commanded by the risen Lord: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19). It signifies the believer’s union with Christ in His death and resurrection, the washing away of sin, and engrafting into His body. The Supper was instituted by Christ on the night He was betrayed, when He took bread and the cup and said, “Take, eat; this is my body… this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Mat 26:26–28). In it the church shows the Lord’s death till He come (1Co 11:23–26), and believers feed upon Christ by faith, receiving His spiritual presence and the renewal of covenant communion. Peter joined repentance and baptism in the first gospel call (Act 2:38). Both ordinances are signs that point beyond themselves to Christ crucified and risen, seals that pledge to faith the grace they signify, and means by which the Lord nourishes His people.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The two ordinances of Christ, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, signs and seals of the covenant of grace.

expand to see more

SACRAMENTS (ORDINANCES), the two holy signs Christ appointed for His church.

Baptism, commanded by the risen Lord, signifies union with Christ (Mat 28:19).

The Lord’s Supper, instituted the night He was betrayed, shows His death (Mat 26:26–28).

They are signs and seals of the covenant, not bare ceremonies.

In them believers feed on Christ by faith and are strengthened (1Co 11:23–26).

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Mat 26:26 — "And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body."

Act 2:38 — "Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost."

1Co 11:26 — "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Rome’s transubstantiation and seven-sacrament system and the doctrine of baptismal regeneration corrupt the ordinances, as does bare memorialism that empties them of Christ’s spiritual presence.

expand to see more

The Roman church corrupted the ordinances in several ways. It multiplied the two Christ appointed into seven, adding confirmation, penance, extreme unction, orders, and marriage to baptism and the Supper without warrant of His institution. It taught transubstantiation, that the bread and wine cease to be bread and wine and become the very body and blood of Christ in substance, so that the Mass is offered anew as a propitiatory sacrifice — a doctrine that contradicts Hebrews’ one offering once for all and turns the Supper into an idolatrous re-sacrificing of Christ. It taught baptismal regeneration, that the water itself confers the new birth apart from faith, making the sign the thing signified. The Reformation recovered the two ordinances of Christ as signs and seals received by faith, not works that save by their bare performance.

The opposite error must also be rejected. Bare Zwinglian memorialism reduces the Supper to a mere remembrance, a token of bread and wine signifying nothing but a past event, denying that Christ is truly present to faith and truly feeds His people in the ordinance. Against both Rome and the bare-memorial view, the dictionary holds the Reformed position: the Supper is a sign and seal in which the believer, by faith, spiritually feeds upon the crucified and risen Christ and is knit afresh into covenant communion with Him. The ordinances do not save by their working; neither are they empty. They are Christ’s appointed means of grace, where He meets His people.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two ordinances of Christ, baptism and the Supper, signs and seals of the covenant of grace.

expand to see more

Sacramentum — Latin, a sacred oath or pledge.

Baptism — commanded by the risen Lord (Mat 28:19).

Lord’s Supper — instituted the night Christ was betrayed (Mat 26:26).

Sign — visibly setting forth the benefits of Christ.

Seal — pledging to faith the grace it signifies.

Usage

"The ordinances preach Christ to the eye as the word preaches Him to the ear."

"Receive the Supper by faith, feeding on Christ, not by a bare remembrance nor a Romish re-sacrifice."

"Baptism marks the believer’s union with Christ; it does not regenerate by the water itself."
